sources.title: Vega: Learning to Drive with Natural Language Instructions

omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.
The retained PDF figures and tables were subsequently inspected on pages 1–9; reference pages 10–13 were read as text. No appendix is present in this 13-page PDF.

Identity/version: the observed title and all six authors match the catalog. The title page identifies arXiv:2603.25741v2 [cs.CV], 30 March 2026. The catalog records submission on 26 March 2026. This report reads v2; v1 and a revision history were not supplied, so changes between versions were not assessed.
The code and project links printed in the paper were not opened. No code was inspected and no experiments were reproduced. No separate supplement was supplied.

synopsis: Vega learns instruction-conditioned driving by training trajectory denoising together with future-image denoising. Modality-specific transformers exchange information through global causal attention. InstructScene supplies automatically generated instructions describing recorded driving. The strongest reported NAVSIM v2 score uses best-of-six trajectory selection; NAVSIM v1 results are weaker than leading VLA baselines. Future-prediction ablations support visual supervision, while selected images illustrate instruction sensitivity without measuring general instruction-following reliability.

problem.text: An averaged imitation policy or a small navigation-command vocabulary cannot express all user-requested driving behaviors. The authors argue that sparse trajectory supervision makes mapping rich visual-language inputs to actions difficult. Vega adds future visual prediction as dense supervision; the claim that this teaches causal dynamics is stronger than the behavioral evidence.

contributions.text: InstructScene pairs NAVSIM scenes with automatically generated driving instructions: 85,109 training scenes and 12,144 test scenes. Annotation combines a VLM with rule-derived ego-motion cues.

An integrated autoregressive-diffusion model uses separate understanding, generation and action transformers with global attention across their token sequence. Joint action/image losses connect planning to action-conditioned visual outcomes.

inputs: Four front-camera history/current images in the reported training setup; VAE and SigLIP2 representations
Historical actions in the interleaving formulation/ablation; their use in the headline configuration is ambiguous
outputs: Eight future relative actions representing planar trajectory motion
A future front-camera image at the action horizon, when image generation is requested

steps.name: Construct instructions from demonstrations
steps.detail: Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct receives 14 front-view frames at 2 Hz and 1920 × 1080 resolution. Four are history/current observations; ten are future annotation inputs unavailable to the deployed agent. Two stages describe the scene and subsequent behavior, then formulate an instruction. Speed, acceleration and turn-rate rules supplement ego-motion perception.

steps.name: Encode observations, language and motion
steps.detail: Qwen2.5 tokenizes instructions. Front-view images provide VAE latents plus SigLIP2 ViT features. Absolute planar trajectory poses become consecutive relative movements, A = (Δx, Δy, Δθ), normalized and linearly projected into action tokens. Normalization constants are not supplied.

steps.name: Connect specialized transformers
steps.detail: Understanding and image-generation transformers have hidden size 3584 and 28 layers, initialized from Bagel-7B; the action module uses width 256. Attention and feed-forward parameters are modality-specific. Segments pass through their respective modules and are reassembled for global attention, providing architectural integration beyond a shared loss.

steps.name: Preserve the conditioning order
steps.detail: Blocks attend causally across the sequence; image/action tokens use full within-block attention, whereas text uses causal within-block attention. Targets that also condition later predictions receive separate noisy and clean copies. Later tokens are masked from the noisy copy and use the clean condition.

training.text: Single-stage joint training predicts an action sequence and its endpoint image using noise-prediction MSE losses. Text, ViT, clean VAE and clean action tokens are randomly dropped by modality for classifier-free guidance. Figure 3 marks the VAE with a snowflake; the text does not enumerate a complete freezing policy.

Training uses 200,000 steps on eight H20 GPUs, per-device batch size one, learning rate 2 × 10⁻⁵, 2,500 warmup steps, equal action/image loss weights, and EMA decay 0.9999 for saved checkpoints. Four images condition eight actions and an endpoint image.

inference.text: Actions are denoised with image and text classifier-free guidance. For joint visualization, a future image is then denoised conditioned on the completed action plan. Inference primarily uses action planning; the source does not describe selecting trajectories by scoring generated futures or an inverse-dynamics controller.
Dagger-marked benchmark variants use best-of-N with N = 6. Trajectory prediction and simulated evaluation do not establish physical vehicle execution.

equations.explanation: Equation (7): A_t^(N) is the N-action plan, I_t^(-T) the image history through the current image, and L_t the instruction. Gaussian noise ε and random diffusion timestep m index action denoising; ε̂ is predicted noise.

Equation (8) and the joint objective: F^V_(t+N) denotes future-image VAE latents; n is the image diffusion timestep. Image denoising additionally conditions on the action plan. Both loss weights are 1.0. These are denoising objectives, not an explicit measured causal-consistency loss.

results.setting: Reported NAVSIM v2 benchmark, described as using reactive traffic. Separate v2 split counts are not supplied. Ordinary and best-of-six variants are reported separately.
results.metric: Extended Predictive Driver Model Score (EPDMS), higher is better
results.comparison: Table 1 reports DriveVLA-W0 at 86.1 and DiffusionDrive at 84.5. Vega† improves over ordinary Vega by 2.5 score points.
results.interpretation: Best aggregate among listed rows, with extra candidate selection for the dagger variant. Components have different leaders: ordinary Vega DAC is 95.3 versus DriveVLA-W0’s 99.1. No uncertainty is reported.

results.setting: NAVSIM test split, non-reactive simulation at 10 Hz for four seconds; Vega uses one front camera. Dagger rows use best-of-six.
results.metric: Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS), higher is better
results.interpretation: Vega is competitive but not the leading VLA in this table. Sensor inputs and training recipes differ. PDMS and EPDMS are different metrics.

results.setting: Section 4.4 ablation on NAVSIM v1/v2; eight H20 GPUs and otherwise Section 4.2 hyperparameters. These are ablation scores, not headline scores.
results.value: Next Frame: 77.9 / 76.0; Random Frame: 77.3 / 75.2; Action Only: 51.8 / 48.9.
results.comparison: Next Frame exceeds Action Only by 26.1 / 27.1 score points, but Random Frame by only 0.6 / 0.8.
results.interpretation: Supports visual prediction supervision within this comparison. The source does not reconcile its baseline with higher headline scores or resolve all horizon terminology.

results.setting: Table 4 compares the image diffusion module, understanding VLM, or dedicated action expert for planning.
results.value: Action Expert: 77.9 / 76.0; Use VLM: 77.6 / 75.7; Use Diffusion: 19.7 / 19.6.
results.comparison: The dedicated expert improves over the VLM by 0.3 points on each score.
results.interpretation: The large gap concerns reusing the image diffusion module. The small VLM gap lacks error bars; a compute benefit is argued but not measured here.

limitations.text: Instruction following and image consistency use selected examples without dedicated quantitative adherence or image-quality evaluation. NAVSIM scores do not isolate compliance with novel requests, and annotations describe recorded futures. These results do not establish causal dynamics identification or real-world deployment safety.

Section 3.3 places past actions in history, but Section 4.4 calls image-only history the original design. The interleaving discussion also describes both equal and differing sequence lengths. Figure 4 measures training log-loss, not driving performance, so convergence alone cannot resolve the planning effect.

The authors attribute weaker NAVSIM v1 performance partly to metrics favoring risk-averse policies and competitors’ extra sensors or training; these explanations are not isolated experimentally. No dedicated limitations section, multi-seed uncertainty, or measured inference latency is supplied.

reproduction.text: Reproduction needs the annotated NAVSIM splits, annotation pipeline, Bagel-7B initialization, SigLIP2/VAE encoders, relative-action normalization, and clean/noisy token mask. Exact prompts, motion-rule thresholds, normalization constants, diffusion schedule/step count, guidance scales, complete freezing policy, software versions and best-of-six selection implementation are unspecified here.

Proposed checks should fix initialization, data, optimization and candidate selection while removing future prediction, then evaluate alternative instructions on identical observations. Resolve the headline/ablation gap before claiming numerical reproduction. These are proposed experiments, not reproduced results.

reasoning.text: Every recorded category is unassigned, leaving no positive catalog classification to confirm. Reader assessment: layerwise global attention supports an integrated One Model interpretation despite modality-specific parameters. The mechanism is jointly trained action prediction and action-conditioned future prediction, ordered action-to-image at inference; it is neither inverse dynamics nor demonstrated future-rollout search for control.

discussionQuestions: Does visual supervision improve adherence when instructions describe valid alternatives to the recorded future?
How much of the best-of-six gain depends on selection rather than the learned planning distribution?
Which history, frame-horizon and checkpoint configurations produced headline versus ablation scores?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author/affiliation block and arXiv margin stamp
evidence.detail: Title: Vega: Learning to Drive with Natural Language Instructions. Authors: Sicheng Zuo, Yuxuan Li, Wenzhao Zheng, Zheng Zhu, Jie Zhou and Jiwen Lu. Affiliations: Tsinghua University and GigaAI. Stamp: arXiv:2603.25741v2 [cs.CV], 30 Mar 2026.

The paper motivates open-ended instructional driving, describes sparse action supervision as a difficulty, and proposes joint image generation and planning to learn instruction/action/outcome relationships.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 3.1 annotation paragraph; p. 6, Section 4.2, Instruction Annotation
evidence.detail: The two-stage Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct pipeline uses 14 front-camera frames at 2 Hz and 1920 × 1080, four past/current and ten future, plus motion rules. It annotates 85,109 train and 12,144 test scenes. Future images are unavailable to the agent at inference. Exact prompts and rule thresholds are not listed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.3, Encoding Inputs and Constructing Input Sequence
evidence.detail: Qwen2.5 tokens, VAE latents and SigLIP2 features encode inputs. Relative normalized planar movement is projected with a linear head. The described sequence includes historical images/actions and a noisy action target or clean action plus noisy image target.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 3.3, Integrated Transformer
evidence.detail: Figure 3 shows understanding/action/generation modules, noisy and clean action tokens, causal attention and a snowflake beside VAE. MoT duplicates attention and FFN parameters. Understanding/generation use width 3584, depth 28 and Bagel-7B initialization; action width is 256. Segments are reassembled for global attention.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.3, sequence construction and paragraphs before Integrated Transformer
evidence.detail: Block-causal attention combines with within-block text causality or full image/action attention. Training duplicates noisy targets and clean conditions, masking noisy copies from subsequent tokens. Inference denoises actions before images, conditioning the latter on fully denoised actions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.4, Equations (7)–(8) and training/inference paragraphs
evidence.detail: Action noise prediction conditions on image history and instruction; image noise prediction also conditions on the action plan. Their weighted MSE sum is optimized jointly. Modality dropout enables classifier-free guidance; inference primarily performs action planning with image/text guidance.

Training uses 200k steps, eight H20 GPUs, four history images, eight predicted actions and an endpoint image, learning rate 2e-5, 2500 warmup steps, per-device batch size one, equal loss weights 1.0 and EMA 0.9999.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1, Datasets and Benchmarks
evidence.detail: NAVSIM v1 uses train/test splits and non-reactive 10 Hz simulation for four seconds with PDMS; v2 is described as enabling reactive traffic and using EPDMS with additional compliance and comfort metrics.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 1, EPDMS and DAC columns, Vega/Vega† and baseline rows; dagger note
evidence.detail: Vega scores 86.9 EPDMS and Vega† 89.4; dagger means best-of-N, N=6. DriveVLA-W0 scores 86.1 and DiffusionDrive 84.5. Vega DAC is 95.3 against DriveVLA-W0 99.1. Vega† has the highest listed aggregate, but components have different leaders.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 2, Sensors and PDMS columns and dagger note; Section 4.3 continuation
evidence.detail: Vega and Vega† use one front camera and score 87.9 and 89.8 PDMS. AutoVLA and AutoVLA† score 89.1 and 92.1 with three cameras; DriveVLA-W0† scores 93.0 with one. The authors discuss metrics, sensors and extra training as potential reasons for weaker v1 performance.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 3 and Section 4.4, Future Frame Prediction
evidence.detail: Random Frame scores 77.3/75.2, Action Only 51.8/48.9, and Next Frame 77.9/76.0 PDMS/EPDMS. The random variant selects one of eight future frames and specifies its index in text. All use eight H20 GPUs and otherwise Section 4.2 hyperparameters; the source does not reconcile these scores with Tables 1–2.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 4; p. 8, Section 4.4, Independent Action Module
evidence.detail: Use Diffusion, Use VLM and Action Expert score 19.7/19.6, 77.6/75.7 and 77.9/76.0. The authors argue that the narrower expert reduces action computation; the table has no runtime, compute measurements or uncertainty.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 4 and Interleaving Observation and Action; p. 8, continuation of that paragraph
evidence.detail: Figure 4 plots log(loss) against fine-tuning steps for original, 2VA, 4VA and 6VA. Interleaved variants start above original and end below it. Prose identifies image-only history as original, describes four images interleaved with three actions, and gives inconsistent equal/differing sequence-length statements.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figure 5 and Section 4.4 Visualizations/VLA Baseline; p. 9, Figure 6 and Conclusion
evidence.detail: Selected scenes show instruction-dependent speed/trajectory changes and sequentially generated future images. Figure 6 includes current images, expert actions, recorded +4s futures and three instruction-conditioned alternatives per scene. Qualitative consistency is claimed, without an aggregate instruction-adherence or image-quality metric.
